entries.title: D.C. Pipe Bomber Suspect Challenges His Statements to the FBI
entries.summary: Attorneys for Brian Cole Jr. say his autism played into a confession.
entries.content:
Defense attorneys for the man accused of being the 2021 D.C. pipe bomber want to block prosecutors from using statements he made during an FBI interrogation last year, saying the autistic man was “broken” by agents who pressured him into a confession after repeated denials.

In a 42-page court filing, Brian Cole Jr.’s lawyers described what they called “his deteriorating mental state” as federal agents pressured him to confess during a December 2025 interrogation and threatened to “drag” his family through a similar experience.

Pointing to a transcript of the interrogation, defense lawyers recounted that Cole told agents: “I did not place the devices. I did not place them … I’m maintaining my innocence … I didn’t, I didn’t place the bombs … How am I supposed to explain that I’m innocent?”

Cole explained to agents that he’s “super introversive” and has “trouble even maintaining a conversation like this” — a character trait that could be particularly acute for someone with autism — but agents pressed on, his lawyers say.

“Lying to federal agents is breaking the law. That’s another crime … so more lies just makes it worse, okay?” one agent said, according to the filing. “No, look at me. Do you understand that?”

John Glover, one of five defense lawyers listed in the court filing, is asking for an evidentiary hearing to discuss their motion to keep the Justice Department from using Cole’s interview with investigators.

Lawyers wrote: “Alone in the interrogation room, shivering while wrapped in the blanket, he chanted to himself: ‘I didn’t, I didn’t, I didn’t, I didn’t. … [E]ven a small chance … Even a small, tiny chance. Smallest, tiniest chances. … Do whatever you can to clear your name. You can get out of this.’”

“This was ‘stimming’ — the self-regulating repetition characteristic of an autistic person in acute physical and emotional distress,” lawyers wrote.

The DOJ accuses Cole of being the mysterious, masked person wearing a hoodie who is seen on camera the night before MAGA protesters descended on the nation’s capital Jan. 6, when pipe bombs were discovered outside the headquarters of both the Democratic and Republican national committees.

When Cole was asked repeatedly whether he recognized the person in the footage of the D.C. pipe bomber — initially saying no, then finally switching to yes — agents congratulated him on being “brave,” the filing states.

“It’s over. Take a breath. Take a breath. It’s over. Let your mind breathe, okay? ... Cry, do whatever you have. It’s over. It’s over, okay? We can resolve this case,” agents said, according to snippets of the transcript included in the court filing.

Cole’s trial is tentatively set to begin in February before U.S. District Judge Amir Ali. He initially was indicted on charges of interstate transportation of explosives and malicious attempt to use explosives, but a second, superseding indictment, charged him with attempting to use weapons of mass destruction and violating a local D.C. code by engaging in an act of terrorism.

FBI investigators were stumped for years and made little progress in the case, and their inaction fueled conspiracy theories that pointed to a former Capitol Police officer and others — including then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia.

Dan Bongino, a conservative podcaster who fed into those theories by proclaiming that the pipe bomb placement was an “inside job” and that the government was engaged in a “massive cover-up,” was selected as the second Trump administration’s No. 2 at the FBI, where he made the investigation a top priority and claimed to closely monitor its progress.

Agents scrapped the previous approach and took a closer look at purchases near D.C. of items that matched the pipe bombs — including galvanized pipes at two different Home Depot stores and white kitchen timers at a Walmart.

They announced a breakthrough on Dec. 4, hours after arresting Cole, and Bongino quickly distanced himself from previous far-fetched theories about the suspect.

However, Cole’s defense lawyers are currently seeking to further probe evidence related to the people who had previously come under public scrutiny. For example, his lawyers have subpoenaed former U.S. Capitol Police officer Shauni Kerkhoff, who sued the right-wing media outlet The Blaze for defamation — noting in court documents that “the FBI interviewed her and administered a polygraph examination that asked her, twice and directly, whether she placed the pipe bombs. She failed it.”

A recent joint status report filed in court by prosecutors and Cole’s defense team pointed out that the government has already turned over information about a “gait-analysis” conducted by a forensic podiatrist named Dr. Michael Nirenberg that reviewed video footage of the pipe bomber.
entries.author: Jose Pagliery

entries.title: Senators Have a Bipartisan Permitting Reform Deal but Little Time to Pass It
entries.summary: Lawmakers have been negotiating for months on the bill, which nearly fell apart several times.
entries.content:
Senators released a long-awaited bipartisan bill Wednesday that could reshape the permitting process for infrastructure and energy projects from gas pipelines to wind turbines.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is aimed at overhauling the processes those projects go through to get approved for construction.

The four main negotiators of the deal — Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) and Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico) — laid out a massive vision for the impact of the bill, which they said would help with everything from building more clean energy and creating new jobs to boosting the entire American economy.

“We're motivated by one central shared concern: We want to make it easier in America to build things,” Lee said at a press conference announcing the deal.

The bill includes provisions meant to make permitting more certain for developers and support the construction of more transmission lines. The legislation would also set limitations on how people can legally challenge new projects under the National Environmental Policy Act. Lawsuits would need to be filed within 150 days of a project’s approval, and those suing would need to have participated in the project’s public comment period.

Data centers developers would be required under the legislation to pay for all the costs associated with grid upgrades, a move that would go further than the Ratepayer Protection Act lawmakers failed to advance Wednesday.

The legislation faces an uphill battle. With the House gone from Washington until after the midterms, only a few short legislative weeks remain before January, when leadership shakeups could scuttle a deal.

“Sometimes big things can happen in lame duck,” Capito said. “We’re banking on it.”

The deal appeared nearly to fall apart several times in the lead-up to Wednesday’s press conference, including earlier that morning over language around offshore wind projects.

The question of whether permitting would return to normal for wind and solar projects, many of which have been blocked under the Trump administration, is still “unresolved,” Whitehouse told reporters.

“But we have had what I would consider to be a very reasonable opening proposal from the Trump administration,” he said. “We need more clarity on that.”

Concessions offered by the White House earlier this month on renewable project permitting bolstered negotiations. The Trump administration has attacked multiple solar and wind projects already in the permitting process, creating a serious hurdle to reforms that both sides pledged would finally come to fruition. Trump has rescinded approvals for major energy projects, issued stop-work orders and cut deals to kill offshore wind development, and terminated grants for other clean energy infrastructure.

Lawmakers have struggled for years to break partisan gridlock on how to reform the U.S. permitting process. Despite widespread agreement that the process of building infrastructure involves too much red tape, Congress hasn’t been able to find common ground on how much of that tape to cut.

A narrower bipartisan bill negotiated in 2024 between Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyoming) and then-Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia made similar moves, but never made it out of the Natural Resources Committee.

Aidan Mackenzie, an infrastructure fellow with the Institute for Progress, called the new deal “easily the best permitting bill we’ve ever gotten.”

For Republicans, the promise of permitting reform includes quicker construction of fossil fuel infrastructure and AI data centers, a focus for the Trump administration. For Democrats, it’s a path toward boosting solar, wind and battery storage projects, along with the transmission lines essential for transporting more electricity.

In a reflection of the widespread interest in permitting reform, both the American Petroleum Institute and Americans for a Clean Energy Grid put out statements in support of the bill.

The response hasn’t been unanimously positive, though. The Conservation Law Foundation called the bill a “backroom energy deal,” saying it would put communities and clean energy at risk.

“The more than 400-page bill appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list, with passage slated before Christmas, sacrificing numerous protections for communities and the environment to achieve outcomes wholly dependent on President Trump’s highly qualified, pre-election assurances that his administration will act in good faith and allow clean energy projects to move forward,” said Conservation Law Foundation President Brad Campbell.

Rose Luttenberger Caruso, advocacy director at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, said passing permitting reform is the biggest clean-energy-related movement possible in the current political environment.

“We are very focused on getting more clean energy online, and the current permitting system just takes way too long to do that,” she said. “It is something that will go a long way for both parties. It’ll help the president’s energy agenda, and it’ll also help bring more sources of clean energy online.”

The House passed several bipartisan permitting reform bills at the end of last year that would have eased requirements under NEPA and the Clean Water Act. On Wednesday, the Senate negotiators said their bill incorporates some language from the House.

The window to pass any kind of permitting reform may slam shut come January, when committee leadership changes and longtime negotiators leave their posts.

If Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) moves to the Judiciary Committee as expected, Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon) is next in line to be his party’s leader on the Environment and Public Works Committee. Merkley, a climate-focused progressive, has raised concerns about permitting reform compromising environmental reviews.

“If it does not happen this Congress, I do not feel that it will happen until 2029 at the earliest,” Luttenberger Caruso said.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian, Anna Kramer

entries.title: FTC Opens a Probe Into OpenAI and Anthropic Over Possible Risks to Consumers
entries.summary: The investigation comes as developers raise concerns about the dangers of AI.
entries.content:
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence companies over dangers their technology may pose to consumers, the agency said Wednesday.

The AI giants and other tech companies in recent months have disclosed examples of their AI agents going beyond human instructions, finding their way onto the internet and hacking external websites.

An FTC spokesperson confirmed the investigation but declined further comment. The investigation was first reported by the New York Post, which said it has been underway for months.

Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to messages for comment on Wednesday.

Concerns around the dangers powerful AI models may pose to humanity have led some of the top AI developers to call for a slowdown. The CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, said this month that the industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.

OpenAI, meanwhile, recently delayed the launch of its newest model this week over safety concerns.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Marsha Blackburn Sues Jack Smith for $1
entries.summary: The Tennessee Republican is seeking a symbolic sum in nominal damages from Smith.
entries.content:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn sued former special counsel Jack Smith on Wednesday over his office’s subpoena for her phone records during its investigation into President Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

The Tennessee Republican is seeking a symbolic sum of $1 in nominal damages from Smith personally. She also wants a federal court to declare his appointment unconstitutional and order her records returned or destroyed.

The lawsuit came one day after Smith defended his move to obtain Republican lawmakers’ phone records during a contentious Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

Sen. Bill Hagerty, another Tennessee Republican whose records were obtained, separately filed a professional misconduct complaint against Smith on Wednesday. He asked the Tennessee Supreme Court’s disciplinary board to investigate Smith and pursue disbarment.

Hagerty alleges Smith withheld key information from a federal court, leading to it approving an order that prevented Verizon from telling him about the subpoena.

Smith defended the nondisclosure orders Tuesday, saying his office followed federal law and Justice Department policy.

In May 2023, Smith’s office issued a grand jury subpoena to Verizon for Blackburn’s toll records. The records show who communicated, when and for how long, but not what was said. The subpoena sought records from Jan. 4 through Jan. 7, but Blackburn’s lawsuit says Verizon inadvertently turned over records from Jan. 1 through Jan. 4 instead.

Smith told senators that investigators sought lawmakers’ records to understand the scope of the alleged conspiracy and who Trump and his allies were trying to influence as they sought to delay certification of the 2020 election. He said the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section approved the process.

In the lawsuit, Blackburn argues Smith had no authority to subpoena her records because his appointment by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland violated the Constitution’s Appointments Clause. She also accuses Smith of violating her constitutional and civil rights in obtaining the records.

The conservative legal group New Civil Liberties Alliance filed the lawsuit on her behalf in federal court in Tennessee.

“Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation’s history,” Blackburn said in a statement on Wednesday, referring to the official name of the federal investigation into Trump’s attempts to stay in power following his 2020 election loss.

Blackburn alleges Smith’s office did not tell the judge who approved the nondisclosure order that the subpoena sought a sitting senator’s records. She argues the secrecy prevented her from challenging the demand and asserting protections under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause.

Blackburn and Hagerty were among the Republican lawmakers whose records were sought during Arctic Frost, the FBI investigation that later became part of Smith’s 2020 election case against Trump.

Smith brought two federal cases against Trump, one over the 2020 election and another over classified documents. Both ended after Trump won the 2024 election because of the Justice Department’s longstanding position that a sitting president cannot be prosecuted.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: The Defense Department Has Spent $49M Feeding the National Guard in D.C.
entries.summary: It’s the latest figure ratcheting up the estimated cost of the Guard’s presence in D.C.
entries.content:
The Department of Defense has spent over $49 million since October 2025 feeding National Guard members posted in D.C. It could spend another $20 million by the end of the year.

The money was spent on catered “breakfast, lunch, dinner and midnight meals” for National Guard members deployed to D.C. as part of President Donald Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force and Freedom 250 celebrations, according to four government contracts reviewed by The Washington Sun. One of the contract solicitations, covering a monthlong period over the summer for $9.9 million, said it would provide 13,200 meals a day.

It’s the latest figure ratcheting up the estimated price tag on the Guard’s presence in D.C., which has spurred protests from residents and D.C. Council members and ongoing litigation from the city’s attorney general. What started as a deployment of 800 troops — largely from the D.C. National Guard — expanded as of early August to 4,630 troops, and will continue through the remainder of Trump’s term.

The cost of activating, deploying and compensating 1,000 troops to a city would be $18 million to $21 million a month, the Congressional Budget Office estimated in January. The federal government recently announced it would spend $292 million housing troops in 2,000 “apartment-style lodging units” around the city through June 2027.

Three of the contracts have ended in the last year, and one still has an unspent $20 million through the end of the year. It’s unclear how much it will cost to feed troops through 2029 — these contracts largely cover a ramped-up presence of almost 5,000 troops over the summer.

The National Guard; Sardi’s Catering, a College Park-based caterer contracted for over $33 million of the work; and Bodwé-KVG JV, a Michigan-based federal contractor awarded a contract for up to $35.7 million, did not immediately respond to questions about the contracts or any further catering contracts the Defense Department has secured.
entries.author: Zara Norman

entries.title: Trump Says the Fallout From His Immigration Crackdown Has Been ‘Tough’
entries.summary: The president told the mostly Latino audience that enforcing his immigration policies has been “the hardest job” he’s had.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he struggles with finding the right balance on immigration enforcement in a rare admission Wednesday.

Speaking to a largely Latino audience at the White House’s Hispanic Heritage Month celebration, Trump touted his administration’s hard-line deportation agenda, but said that the job weighs on him.

“Frankly, it's the hardest job I've had. The hardest job, because they'll say you're too tough or you're too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it's always tough,” he told the audience.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests hit record highs last month as the administration continues to escalate its aggressive enforcement policies, which include mass deportations, family separations at the border and sweeping restrictions on both legal asylum processes and refugee admissions.

Trump’s approval ratings among Hispanics have also dropped in the two years since he won a second term with new levels of support among Latino voters.

Trump has seldom budged on his alarmist rhetoric against immigration from Latin American countries. After ICE agents shot two American citizens in Minneapolis during the administration’s Operation Metro Surge immigration crackdown, he showed some vulnerability.

“I learned that maybe we could use a little bit of a softer touch. But you still have to be tough,” Trump told NBC News in February.

Trump directed the withdrawal of 700 immigration agents from Minnesota following those incidents and the resulting political unrest.

The president’s statements Wednesday echoed that change — but didn’t last long. He soon pivoted to his longtime claims that foreign countries are emptying prisons and mental institutions into the United States.

He also returned to another recurring midterms pitch, telling the audience to “believe” he’s also on the ballot: “We lose 40% when I don't run.”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Troy Jackson Walks Back His Comment on Jewish Mainers' Views on Gaza
entries.summary: The Democratic candidate for Senate said he had made a “generalization” about residents’ views.
entries.content:
Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson apologized on Wednesday for any “pain” caused by a comment he made about Jewish residents’ views on the war in Gaza.

On Tuesday, Jackson said it is “unfortunate” that members of the Jewish community in his state do not call the ongoing conflict in the Gaza Strip a “genocide.”

“It’s unfortunate that there are people here in Maine that don’t like to use that term, only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust,” he said in an interview with News Center Maine. 

Jackson also said that “senseless murders, horrific murders, are happening to both sides” of the conflict between the Israeli and Palestinian people, specifically criticizing Hamas.

In a statement shared with The Washington Sun on Wednesday, Jackson walked back some of his comments and said residents of his state hold a “range of deeply considered views.”

“I believe what’s happening in Gaza is genocide, and I also understand that word carries particular weight for many Jewish families given the Holocaust — the genocide of six million Jews,” Jackson said. “In trying to acknowledge that, I misspoke and made a generalization about Jewish Mainers’ views that doesn't reflect what I meant to say.”

He also committed to fighting antisemitism and working “for lasting peace and security for Palestinians and Israelis” if elected to the Senate.

Jackson became the Democratic pick for the Senate race in July after former nominee Graham Platner’s campaign imploded over accusations of sexual assault and violence against his former partners. The former state lawmaker hopes to unseat five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November.

Jackson has repeatedly referred to the conflict in the Gaza Strip and the subsequent death toll of the Palestinian people as a “genocide.” Platner, who was known for his progressive views, also explicitly referred to the war in Gaza as a “genocide.”

Collins has voiced concerns for the the treatment of both Palestinians and Israelis in the ongoing conflict, but she has previously stopped short of calling it a “genocide.” The senator has also been a staunch advocate for Israel’s “right to defend itself” in the past.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Former Rep. Adam Kinzinger Under Investigation for Kalshi Trades
entries.summary: The Illinois Republican has not responded to the prediction market’s attempts to contact him about the probe, according to a source familiar with the investigation.
entries.content:
Kalshi has referred an investigation into trades made by former Republican Rep. Adam Kinzinger to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency tasked with regulating the popular prediction market, according to a source close to Kalshi.

The agency subsequently opened up its own investigation into Kinzinger in connection with bets he placed on whether he would receive a pardon from President Joe Biden — which he eventually did — according to Politico.

Kinzinger has not responded to several attempts by Kalshi to notify him about the investigation and ask for his cooperation, the source familiar with the investigation told The Washington Sun.

In a statement shared with The Washington Sun, the former congressman, who remains a strong critic of President Donald Trump, connected the investigation to a larger attempt by the administration and Kalshi to target him for “less than $1000 in legal bets I made as a private citizen.”

Kinzinger also refuted claims that he had not responded to the inquiries and said he had no insider knowledge about potentially getting a pardon from Biden.

“I have received no communications from the CFTC or Kalshi and will cooperate with any investigation to prove my obvious innocence,” Kinzinger wrote.

The investigation stems from trades the former congressman made in December 2024, the month before he received a presidential pardon, according to the source.

Kinzinger previously called Kalshi a “corruption time bomb” and has been critical of the role prediction markets can play in affecting the behavior of members of Congress.

“This system essentially invites public officials, staff, donors, or anyone in the orbit of power to cash in on privileged information,” Kinzinger wrote in a November 2025 Substack post. “We already struggle with stock-trading scandals; this is an even cleaner, easier avenue for corruption.”

In his statement, Kinzinger brushed off the investigations and hit back against Kalshi for launching a probe after he criticized the prediction market.

“These bets were done as a hobbyist, similar to a retired athlete betting on the sport he used to play,” he wrote. “It is certainly curious that after I called Kalshi out for potentially turning a blind eye to corruption they have chosen to team up with the Trump Administration to tarnish my reputation for activity that clearly followed their platform guidelines.”

Kinzinger provided screenshots to The Sun showing that he made $823 on the trades.

The CFTC did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and Kalshi declined to comment on the matter.

Kinzinger isn’t the only former member of Congress to face an investigation tied to activity on the prediction market. Former New York Rep. George Santos, who was expelled from Congress in 2023, received Kalshi’s first lifetime ban in August in connection with trades he made on whether he would attend President Donald Trump’s 2026 state of the Union address.

Kinzinger faced Trump’s ire for his role on the House Select Committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Biden preemptively pardoned Kinzinger, several other lawmakers and dozens of congressional aides in the final hours of his term on Jan. 20, 2025, after Trump said those involved with the investigation “should go to jail.”

The Illinois Republican retired from Congress after his term ended in 2023, following a round of redistricting that affected his chances at reelection.

While in Congress, Kinzinger was one of the only 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump in 2021. Since leaving office, he has continued to be openly critical of Trump and the direction of the Republican Party.

This story has been updated with additional comments and information from Adam Kinzinger.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Trump Signs Order to Significantly Reduce Mosquitoes and Ticks in D.C.
entries.summary: Officials have two months to develop a plan to reduce the District’s mosquito population by 90% and tick population by 50% before 2028.
entries.content:
The Trump administration wants to crack down on pests in D.C. — mosquitoes and ticks.

In an executive order Tuesday, President Donald Trump directed federal agencies to work with local officials to reduce the District’s mosquito population by 90% and cut its tick population in half by 2028.

The order directs federal health and environmental officials to submit a plan to Trump within the next two months to develop and release advanced tick and mosquito control technologies on federal property in D.C. That could include “safe genetic modification” and the use of “safe, beneficial bacteria” as well as cleaning tick and mosquito breeding grounds.

“Historical approaches have relied primarily on the use of conventional pesticides,” the order said, “however, the use of commonsense, non-chemical, technology-enabled measures can significantly reduce the negative effects of these pests, enhancing enjoyment of the great outdoors for all Americans.”

At the start of tick season in April, the Northeast experienced the highest weekly rates of ER visits for tick bites since 2017, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At-large D.C. Council member Christina Henderson said in a post on X on Wednesday that the order is “random and yet timely,” as she has had meetings in the past month about mosquitoes, standing water and the need for treatment strategies in the District.

D.C. Health is in charge of mosquito mitigation across D.C., such as treating standing water in public spaces, but not private properties. Capitol Hill residents formed the Itty Bitty Mosquito Population Committee in March in an effort to lower the number of mosquitoes in the neighborhood, The 51st reported.

Mayor Muriel Bowser’s office referred a request for comment to D.C. Health. D.C. Health did not respond to a request for comment before publication.
entries.author: Justice Covert

entries.title: Zimbabwe Rejected a Deal With Trump. Cuts to Health Aid Followed.
entries.summary: The State Department proposed making aid conditional to the country’s ability to access sensitive data from the Zimbabwean government.
entries.content:
The Trump administration officially ended decades of global health aid to Zimbabwe on Wednesday, cutting off funding for HIV and infectious disease prevention efforts after Zimbabwean officials rejected an “America first” health deal.

The affected programs would receive a short period to “responsibly close operations,” a State Department spokesperson told The Washington Post, adding that Washington was “committed to an orderly handover.”

Negotiations over the five-year, $367 million agreement covering HIV, tuberculosis, malaria and other health priorities collapsed in February. The State Department proposed making aid conditional to the U.S.’s ability to access sensitive medical and biological data from the Zimbabwean government, related to a wider push to gain access to valuable mineral stores.

More than 30 countries signed similar agreements with the U.S.

Officials from Zimbabwe, one of a handful of nations that refused the terms, said the proposal failed to guarantee their country would benefit from medical advances developed using that information. Zimbabwean government spokesperson Nick Mangwana called the arrangement “asymmetrical” at its core.

“When financial assistance is contingent upon concessions that touch upon national sovereignty, data sovereignty or access to strategic resources, it fundamentally alters the nature of the relationship from one of partnership to one of unequal exchange. This we cannot accept,” he said in February.

On top of those stipulations, the U.S. officials indicated they were only willing to spend a fraction of what they paid in previous longstanding commitments, while requiring Zimbabwe to more than double its spending on the health programs over the next four years.

U.S. funding has supported salaries and training for 8,300 health workers, along with laboratory services and disease detection capacity at approximately 1,900 facilities, according to Health GAP, an organization that advocates for access to HIV treatment and prevention.

“The human costs will be catastrophic,” the organization’s executive director wrote on Tuesday, urging both governments to resume negotiations and calling for emergency funding to protect critical health services.

The dispute reflects the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to uproot foreign health assistance and last year’s massive cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development — moves officials say are meant to reduce dependence on aid

“We must keep what is good about our health foreign assistance programs while rapidly fixing what is broken,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier this month.

Zimbabwean officials pledged this week to raise government spending and to seek funding from the Global Fund, an organization focused on fighting AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria.

Meanwhile, officials are trying to preserve some critical health services scheduled for the chopping block. The National AIDS Council began reviewing which programs could be absorbed into its national response, adding that the organization would prioritize the procurement and distribution of antiretroviral drugs, according to Zimbabwean media outlet The Herald.

Neither Zimbabwe’s government nor global health nonprofits have the resources to absorb the full cost of the withdrawn U.S. support, according to Health GAP.

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Duffy Calls for Quicker Aviation Certifications to Keep Up With China
entries.summary: The FAA proposed a new rule in June that would make the certification “faster, simpler, and less expensive while maintaining the highest safety standards.”
entries.content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Wednesday called for a quicker certification process for new aircraft from Boeing and other manufacturers with U.S. production to more easily keep up with mounting competition from China.

“Where’s the new innovation in aviation from the ‌big producers? It doesn’t happen ‌because it’s so hard to certify,” Duffy said during a Y Combinator event for startups. “We ⁠need to make sure we have safe aviation, but can we move faster?”

The move to change federal aviation standards could spur increased innovation from some of the major manufacturers operating in the U.S. market, including Boeing, Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier.

“If we can't move at a different pace ⁠in ⁠certification, we're going to lose. ⁠China is going to beat us,” Duffy told reporters after the event, which was hosted in D.C. He also called for “more competition, more players,” in the industry.

The United States ranks first among the world’s aerospace leaders by export valuation, according to 2024 calculations from Tendata, a global trade intelligence platform. France and Germany rank second and third, respectively. China trails behind the U.S. as a competitor — but the country's push in the defense sector has spurred progress for its aviation industry, the online aviation publication Simple Flying reported in February.

In June, the Federal Aviation Administration “issued a proposed rule to make the certification of transport-category airplanes and their propulsion systems faster, simpler, and less expensive while maintaining the highest safety standards,” the agency said in a statement.

Boeing referred The Washington Sun to the FAA’s June statement on the new certification standards. Representatives for Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Certifying new aircraft can take between five to nine years, according to the FAA. Amended type certificates, which federal regulators award to allow a manufacturer to change aircraft that have already been certified, can take three to five years.

The proposed rule would also streamline certification processes by aligning the U.S.’s approach to certification “more closely with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency’s standards,” the FAA said in its statement.

Boeing, which is headquartered in Virginia, has struggled to receive relatively quick certifications for some of its aircraft models in recent years, with the 777X model running seven years behind schedule.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Senate Punts Bill to Permanently Ban Chinese Cars Until After Midterms
entries.summary: The bipartisan measure would ban the import, manufacture and sale of internet-connected vehicles linked to China or other foreign adversaries.
entries.content:
By Joey Cappelletti and Didi Tang

Legislation to permanently ban the sale of Chinese vehicles in the United States stalled out on Wednesday as senators struggled to seal an agreement, virtually guaranteeing that the bill will have to wait until after the November elections.

The bipartisan bill, sponsored by Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio and Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, aims to prevent China’s auto industry from gaining a foothold in the U.S. market. It would ban the import, manufacture and sale of internet-connected vehicles, software and hardware linked to China or other foreign adversaries, including Russia and North Korea.

Chinese automakers are already effectively banned from selling or building vehicles in the U.S. under a policy put into place by the Biden administration, but senators are hoping to more permanently shut the door.

The summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Washington last week, which focused in part on trade between the world’s two largest economies, had given the legislation renewed momentum. Slotkin said nearly every senator was prepared to support it, and they had initially planned to seek passage last week without a formal roll call vote.

Senators delayed action to continue negotiations with the lone holdout, Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who argued the legislation could unfairly sweep in Mercedes-Benz. The bill would bar vehicles made by companies with more than a 15% ownership stake from Chinese entities. Mercedes-Benz has nearly 20% passive Chinese ownership.

Supporters say they will try again after the elections. But the delay is a setback for bipartisan legislation that has drawn support from automakers and labor unions as Washington grapples with the growing global reach of China’s auto industry — and concerns about potential surveillance technology.

“It is literally a driving spy machine on wheels,” Slotkin said of Chinese vehicles. “All of that data and all of that information goes back to Beijing.”

Lawmakers see threat from Chinese EVs

Lawmakers and analysts have warned of dire consequences if Chinese EVs should become available in the U.S.

“I am concerned about what can happen to the U.S. automobile industry with the Chinese electric vehicles,” said Republican Sen. Steve Daines in an interview with The Associated Press before the Trump-Xi summit. “They are remarkable, high quality at a much lower cost. But it’s not fair if you have a product that is significantly subsidized by a government to be able to come into our market."

Chinese automakers have expanded rapidly overseas, competing aggressively on price and technology and putting pressure on established manufacturers in Europe and other markets. In the first eight months of this year, China’s exports of new-energy vehicles more than doubled from the previous year, shipping out more than 3.4 million vehicles, according to China Association of Automobile Manufactures.

Chinese automakers supplied 60% of global electric car sales in 2025, while European and North American automakers were each responsible for about 15% of global sales, according to IEA, or the International Energy Agency.

Their emergence has raised concerns in Detroit that allowing them into the U.S. could expose domestic automakers to a new source of lower-cost competition.

Trump, however, has at times taken a more welcoming approach to Chinese investment in the U.S. auto industry. Speaking at the Detroit Economic Club in January, he said he was open to Chinese automakers building factories in the United States as long as they employed American workers.

“If they want to come in and build the plant and hire you and hire your friends and your neighbors, that’s great. I love that,” Trump said. “Let China come in.”

That position has put Trump at odds with an unusual coalition of lawmakers, automakers and labor unions that has pushed to keep Chinese vehicles out of the U.S. market.

In April 2026, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said “no” when he was asked if Chinese EV makers such as BYD would come and set up joint ventures in the U.S.

But in early September, before he hosted China's Xi, Trump again said he would not oppose Chinese automakers building cars in the United States.

The White House didn’t respond to a request by AP regarding its stance on the bill.

What the bill would do

Slotkin and Moreno have framed their legislation around two threats: protecting the U.S. auto industry from heavily subsidized Chinese competitors and preventing technology embedded in connected vehicles from collecting sensitive data on Americans.

In July, Slotkin called Chinese cars “surveillance packages on wheels,” arguing that they could collect information on American drivers and sensitive sites and transmit it to Beijing. Moreno has said China’s auto industry “was built to destroy American manufacturing, gut the middle class, and undermine our national security.”

The bill would prohibit the import, manufacture, sale, resale or introduction into interstate commerce of connected vehicles and related software and hardware associated with China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. It would effectively write into law and expand restrictions that began under the Biden administration, making it harder for a future administration to reverse them.

But some are concerned that the 15% ownership cap could hurt companies with strong roots in the United States.

“We're not going to have the president of the United States sign a bill — nor would he — that bans Mercedes-Benz from the United States of America,” said Moreno, also mentioning companies like Volvo. “We have to figure out a way to manage all of that.”

James Lewis, a distinguished fellow with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, said the bill could return after the midterm elections, given the threat that Chinese carmakers pose to U.S. companies.

“China can make enough cars in a single year to supply the entire global demand. You don’t need any other countries to make cars with China in the picture,” Lewis said. “This is existential for the car companies.”

“Car companies care a lot. They’re very influential,” he said. “They’re deeply concerned about this.”

entries.title: Trump Defends His Taxpayer-Funded Campaign Ads
entries.summary: “Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money,” the president said Wednesday.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday defended a recent slate of campaign ads that say they were paid for by the U.S. government, arguing the spots are promoting the country rather than his own political interests.

“Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked about criticism that the ads, which began running last week, might violate federal anti-propaganda laws. “I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

His comments follow revelations that Customs and Border Protection had awarded a $20 million contract for a national media campaign days before the ads began airing.

Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticized the spending as potentially illegal and a misuse of taxpayer funds, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who this week called them “a great message” that “shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars.”

“That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” Trump said Wednesday.
